title: Navigating EC2: Finding and Inspecting Instances
intro: EC2 is AWS's virtual machine service, the cloud version of 'a server'. The console is fine for one instance; the CLI is how you work with hundreds. This tutorial covers finding the right instance, reading its state, and seeing why it won't boot without logging in.

steps.prompt: List all running instances as a table of id, Name tag, type, private IP, and public IP, using --query.
steps.explanation: Three running instances. Only web-1 has a public IP.
steps.why: Raw describe-instances output is hundreds of lines of nested JSON (Reservations → Instances → ...). --filters narrows server-side, and --query shapes the output client-side. Learning this one JMESPath pattern saves hours; the Name tag lookup (Tags[?Key==`Name`]|[0].Value) is worth memorising.

steps.prompt: Find the instance whose Name tag is batch-7 by filtering on the tag.
steps.explanation: batch-7 is a c6i.4xlarge launched almost a year ago, owned by data-team.
steps.why: Tags are how organisations find things (and how cost gets allocated). Filter by tag rather than guessing ids. A 16-vCPU instance running for a year with a name like 'batch' is exactly the kind of forgotten resource a cost review finds.

steps.prompt: api-1 (i-0b2c3d4e5f6789012) was reported unresponsive. Check its status checks.
steps.explanation: System status is ok but instance status is impaired: AWS's hardware is fine, but the operating system isn't responding.
steps.why: The two checks split the blame. A failed SYSTEM check is AWS's problem (host hardware or network), fixed by stop/start, which moves the instance to new hardware. A failed INSTANCE check is yours: the OS, kernel, disk or network config. Knowing which one failed tells you whether to wait for AWS or start debugging.

steps.prompt: Read the latest boot console output of i-0b2c3d4e5f6789012 to see why the OS is stuck, without needing to log in.
steps.fake_output:
[  OK  ] Reached target Local File Systems (Pre).
[ TIME ] Timed out waiting for device /dev/xvdf.
[DEPEND] Dependency failed for /data.
[DEPEND] Dependency failed for Local File Systems.
You are in emergency mode. After logging in, type "journalctl -xb" to view system logs
steps.explanation: The boot stopped in emergency mode: /etc/fstab lists /dev/xvdf for /data, and that volume isn't attached.
steps.why: When SSH and SSM are both dead, the console output is the one window into a broken boot. The fix here is 'nofail' in fstab (or mounting by UUID), so a missing data volume can't block the whole boot. aws-incident-005 is this exact failure.

steps.prompt: Stop and start (not reboot) i-0c3d4e5f678901234 to change its type later. First, stop it.
steps.explanation: batch-7 is stopping. Its EBS disks and private IP are kept.
steps.why: Reboot keeps the instance on the same host; stop/start moves it to a new one (which is also the fix for a failed system check), and is required to change the instance type. Stop is not terminate: terminate deletes the instance and, by default, its root volume. Also note that a public IP not backed by an Elastic IP changes on stop/start.
